title: In 76,215 human genomes, strand differences in singleton frequencies of new six-base words in introns largely follow strand-specific mutation linked to transcription, not selection on the RNA
abstract:
New short sequences (words) made by point mutations in human introns are seen once (as singletons) more or less often depending on whether they form on the transcribed (sense) strand or the other strand; these differences largely follow strand-specific mutation rates, not purifying selection on the pre-mRNA. This matters because strand-specific allele-frequency tests are used to find RNA signals that non-coding DNA must avoid, and this mutational effect gives false signals up to half as large as those of strongly predicted cryptic splice sites.

We used 188.8 million single-nucleotide variants in 997.5 Mb of protein-coding introns from gnomAD v4.1 (76,215 genomes). For 2,016 pairs of six-base words, we compared the singleton excess (extra fraction of variants seen once; selection raises it) for words made on the sense strand with that for words made on the antisense strand. In introns, 1,062 pairs differed at a false discovery rate of 5% (up to 2.7 percentage points, pp; replication between genome halves r = 0.86); in intergenic DNA, which has no transcription, none did (r = 0.01). Its amplitude was 0.36 in genes silent in body tissues and testis and 1.29 in genes active in both.

The difference follows the mutated trinucleotide (59 of 96 classes; 1 of 96 in intergenic DNA), is the same in rare variants only and in genes on either reference strand (r = 0.96), and across 1,343 pentanucleotide contexts the singleton contrast follows the variant-density contrast with the slope of recurrent mutation (-6.9; recurrence -5.6; selection about -35). One family, T>C at A-T-[A/T]-G on the sense strand, has up to +10.5 pp that recurrence does not explain; its density deficit is absent in singletons and similar in rare and common variants, which does not fit a single selection coefficient; a recent change of strand bias, non-inherited singleton calls, or a mixture of strongly harmful and neutral mutations remain possible. After allowing for real differences between mutation routes, only one word pair (ACGTAA, 5-prime splice-site-like, +1.15 pp) keeps a contrast that is consistent across models and ancestries. New AATAAA polyadenylation signals in introns show no selection (-0.14 pp, SE 0.08; same-composition words -0.34 to +0.17), which excludes heterozygote selection above about 1e-4 (bound uncertain about two-fold).

Limitations: the T>C outlier is not resolved; ancestral alleles and replication direction were not used; selection below about 1e-4 is not detected.
